The student files with the Registrar’s Office a statement of approval by the dean of the college/school and the chair of the department in which she or he wishes to complete the second degree;

The student’s major for the second degree is taken in a subject matter field other than the one in which she or he was awarded the first degree; and furthermore,

The credit-hour requirements for the major leading to the second baccalaureate degree are those specified in the current catalog and will have been earned after the awarding of the first baccalaureate degree.

In addition, the following regulations apply:

A minimum of 32 credit hours toward the second baccalaureate degree must be completed in residence at the University of Guam.

Students holding a baccalaureate degree from other U.S. accredited four-year colleges and universities or foreign equivalent may attempt a second baccalaureate degree at the University of Guam provided they meet the relevant requirements listed above.

The Western Interstate Commission for Higher Education (WICHE) is a regional organization created by the Western Regional Education Compact and adopted in the 1950s by Western states. WICHE was created to facilitate resource sharing among the higher education systems of the West. Helping students gain affordable access to higher education is one of its objectives.

The Western Undergraduate Exchange (WUE) is coordinated by WICHE. Students enrolled through WUE pay up to 150% of the enrolling institution’s resident undergraduate tuition. To qualify, applicants must demonstrate residency in a WICHE member state and must be admitted to a WUE-eligible major at UOG.

WICHE's member states include 15 Western states and member U.S. Pacific Territories and Freely Associated States (currently, the Republic of Marshall Islands, Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands, Republic of Paulau and Guam). WICHE’s 15 member states are: Alaska, Arizona, California, Colorado, Hawaii, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, North Dakota, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming.

item.title: Tåotao Tritons | All the Right Moves: Brionna June Turns Dance into Passion with Purpose
item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons | All the Right Moves: Brionna June Turns Dance into Passion with Purpose
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | All the Right Moves: Brionna June Turns Dance into Passion with Purpose

Brionna June is used to being on the move. Before joining the University of Guam as a Senior Retention Specialist, the Atlanta native lived, worked, and studied across the U.S. But no matter where June finds herself, a part of her life that remains constant is dance. The life-long passion has literally kept June on her toes and opened doors to countless opportunities and experiences.

June’s love for dance was built on a foundation of performing that can be traced back to when she was as young as three years old.

“My father’s a pastor, so a lot of the stuff that I did, whether it was singing, dancing, acting, whatever, started in church,” June explains. “I loved performing and being in front of people.”

Wanting her daughter to be well-rounded, June’s mom required her to maintain school grades above 95% and join other sports throughout the year in order to keep dancing. June stayed committed and was able to dance all throughout her K-12 journey and well into college.

Along with joining the marching band dance/flag team at Miles College and earning the position of captain by her sophomore year, June expanded her performance resume considerably. She was a background dancer and singer, joined several stage plays, and had bit parts in some TV shows.

Her time in the spotlight, however, wasn’t meant to last for the long haul.

“When I got older, I realized I wasn’t as prepared for the performance world as I thought I was, so I started tapping into preparing the next generation,” June says, a decision that took her from dancer to choreographer.

After graduating from college, June focused her energy into sharing her skills and knowledge. She began hosting dance clinics for the high schools in her county and fell in love with the impact she could make on up-and-coming dancers.

It was especially important for June to provide the dancers with the guidance she wished she had growing up and to “show them different ways they could be better.” That vision led her to opening her own studio in Atlanta, where teams of young dancers honed their skills in hip hop, contemporary, and majorette technique. When she landed a job at San Diego State University (SDSU) several years later, June closed her Atlanta studio and reopened it in the new city, expanding her training ground to West Coast dancers.

Although June’s role as a coach and choreographer shifted her more behind the scenes, it still allowed her to stay connected to dance and continue to express her creativity.

“A dancer does the motion, and the choreographer creates the motion, so that’s always fun trying to find new and exciting ways to keep people interested in watching somebody move,” she says.

June also lent her choreography expertise to larger-scale projects, collaborating with the TV network VH1; rapper and singer Saweetie; and Fenty Beauty, Rihanna’s cosmetics brand, to create original content.

June’s approach to coaching stems from the belief that greatness is born from discipline and tough love. “Coach Bri,” as her dancers call her, finds the most rewarding part of her mentor role in seeing her dancers evolve, not just in their technique, but also in their character.

That evolution often begins with tryouts where June intentionally “shakes the tree” to see who is serious about dancing. The ones who make the team—both those who are already resilient and those who quickly learn to build thick skin—must then face “cuts,” meaning they have to earn their spots for specific performances.

While the goal is to get everyone to push their dancing to the next level, the competitive spirit June likes to foster is meant to be healthy: a dancer can miss out on a spot, congratulate the teammate who got it, and come back determined to earn the spot next time.

“You’re going to compete in life all the time, whether it’s for a job, for a promotion, whether it’s unconsciously, subconsciously,” June tells her dancers, “but it doesn’t have to be ugly. You can just put it all out there, do your best, then move on.”

The results of June’s coaching philosophy speak for themselves. Both her Atlanta and San Diego teams won multiple regional and national competitions. While at SDSU, she coached the SDSU Diamonds, the university’s dance team that became popular for their high-energy performances during athletic games. Today, many of June’s former dancers are professional backup dancers, NFL cheerleaders, or have become coaches and choreographers themselves.

For June, these examples illustrate how success is more than just trophies or titles; they show that her dancers have embodied the core values of putting in the work and loving what they do.

While June has only been at UOG for half a year, she is already making big moves. She is finding ways to motivate students to attend UOG and earn their degrees, but also to enjoy their college experience. Part of that plan has been establishing the Triton Spirit Squad, a student team that uses a fusion of dance and cheerleading to boost campus engagement and school spirit.

Beyond getting students involved in extracurriculars, June’s work is rooted in giving them the kind of support she remembers receiving from academic mentors during her own college days.

“That’s what drew me to both dancing and education, being that example for others,” she shares.

The opportunities to encourage young people remain plentiful for June. Whether she is guiding Tritons as they navigate their college plans or challenging her Spirit Squad members to find their rhythm, June is all about helping students and dancers alike recognize what they are capable of and giving them someone they can look to along the way.

item.title: Tåotao Tritons | Twice the Fight: Mia and Rckaela Aquino Wrestle Their Way Forward
item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons | Twice the Fight: Mia and Rckaela Aquino Wrestle Their Way Forward
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | Twice the Fight: Mia and Rckaela Aquino Wrestle Their Way Forward

For many athletes, the Olympics represent the epitome of competition, the ultimate proving ground of one’s hard work and commitment to their sport. Sisters and University of Guam seniors Mia-Lahnee and Rckaela Aquino know very well what it takes to reach that international stage. They have spent most of their lives training in wrestling to not only represent themselves and their family, but also the island that they call home, and what they have accomplished thus far is proof that grit, focus, and persistence can lead to some pretty amazing places.

Grappling has always run in the Aquino family. Mia and Rckaela’s dad and uncles trained in both judo and wrestling, and their dad aspired to compete in the Olympics. That dream was one he passed down to his daughters.

“As soon as we turned 5 and 4, we just started wrestling, and the rest is history,” says Mia, the older of the two sisters.

The journey, however, was not without its challenges. While Mia viewed wrestling as a passion they were now sharing with their dad, Rckaela initially struggled with the sport.

“I didn’t like it at first, to be honest,” Rckaela reveals. “It was a lot of pressure for me and a lot of crying, and I felt like it was just really hard.”

A turning point came in 2016, when Rckaela accompanied Mia to Mongolia for Mia’s first-ever Olympic qualifier attempt. In the training room, they saw a host of female wrestlers, including World Championship gold medalist Helen Maroulis, who was part of the U.S. team. Being surrounded by such high-caliber talent was eye-opening for Rckaela.

“I was like, ‘Wow, I want that for Guam. I want to do that for Guam,’ and in that moment, the dream became my dream instead of my dad’s,” she says.

Driven by a clear goal and guided by their dad’s coaching, Mia and Rckaela spent over a decade proving their mettle in regional and global competitions, such as the Micronesian Games and the World Wrestling Championships, often medaling in their respective weight classes. They represented Guam in countries all over the world, including New Zealand, Samoa, Kazakhstan, Hungary, and China.

A pivotal milestone was reached when Rckaela qualified for the 2020 Tokyo Olympics. She became the first female athlete from Guam to qualify on merit in any sport.

In wrestling, qualifying on merit means that instead of accumulating points or receiving a pre-assigned spot reserved for a country, spots are earned by winning a designated qualifying tournament outright. For Guam wrestlers, one such tournament is the Africa-Oceania Olympic Qualifier.

In 2024, both Rckaela and Mia made the three-day voyage from Guam to the Africa-Oceania Olympic Qualifier in Egypt. In another triumph, they won their respective brackets and secured their spots to represent the island in Paris, effectively earning the honor of being the first siblings from Guam to qualify on merit for the same Olympic Games in the same sport.

The historic accomplishment was especially meaningful to the sisters. Not only did they finally achieve their dream of making it to the Olympics together, but the journey also reaffirmed their belief that success could be cultivated right at home.

“We were just training on Guam. We didn’t have to move away. It takes a lot, but if we can do it, anyone can,” Mia says. “Coming from a small island, it really showed that no dream is too small and that we qualify here, we belong here.”

Even after making their marks in the last Olympic Games, Mia and Rckaela have refused to become complacent. They train six days a week, sometimes up to two sessions a day. Mornings are for cardio conditioning, while afternoons are dedicated to wrestling techniques and sparring. Each session usually lasts for three to four hours.

Despite the grueling physical demands of the sport, the sisters agree that 99% of wrestling is actually a mental game.

“It’s that whole wrestling mindset: you’re either gonna do it, or you’re not gonna do it. You’re stressed? Okay. You still have to go to training at the end of the day,” Mia says.

For Rckaela, overcoming anxiety before matches, and even before practice, remains a work in progress. “I’m still learning about myself and figuring out how to deal with nerves so that they don’t affect me,” she shares.

The mental toughness the Aquinos have built throughout their athletic careers has also been crucial in helping them balance other aspects of their lives. Along with part-time jobs, they are working towards earning their degrees in Health Science , with Mia emphasizing in Pre-Physical Therapy and Rckaela emphasizing in Exercise Science and Health Promotion.

Family, friends, and even professors at UOG have been sources of external support, providing the encouragement and flexibility the sisters need to manage work, academics, and training. Coupled with their own discipline and determination, the support systems help keep Mia and Rckaela focused on their goals.

The next few years will be busy for the duo. Once they complete their bachelor’s, they hope to hang their grad gowns alongside new sets of Olympic wrestling singlets, as they aim for the 2028 Summer Olympics in Los Angeles. The road to gold won’t be easy, but Mia and Rckaela have walked the path before and understand what exists on the other side of the sacrifices.

“All the long hours at training, all the missed birthdays and family parties—it pays off. It pays off because in the end, we’re on that Olympic stage. Win or lose, we have that title. We can call ourselves Olympians,” Mia declares.

But even beyond personal victories, Mia and Rckaela envision a future in which they give back. They plan on entering healthcare careers where they can offer wellness services like physical therapy and nutrition guidance to athletes. And just as their dad passed on his love for wrestling to them, Mia and Rckaela want to pay that same passion forward to others.

“I would like us to really build the next generation. If we can get more people into wrestling, especially females, that’ll be the greatest for me,” Rckaela says. “Wrestling offers you room to grow more self-confident and to be able to hold your own. It can change lives; it changed mine.”

“Wrestling on Guam is not going to stop at us. It’s going to continue on, even when we leave the sport,” Mia assures. It will be a long while before the Aquinos retire from the mats, but in the meantime, they continue to push forward with the heart and dedication of true champions.

item.description: Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More) Tåotao Tritons | In Tune: Dr. Dean Olah on Living the Dream as a Teacher and Trombonist
item.content:encoded:
Calvo's Donates $3M to UOG Endowment (Read More)

Tåotao Tritons | In Tune: Dr. Dean Olah on Living the Dream as a Teacher and Trombonist

Dr. Dean Olah is a Professor of Education with UOG’s School of Education and a professional trombonist

If you ever find yourself at the University of Guam’s School of Education building early enough in the morning, you might hear rich, brassy melodies echoing through the first-floor hallways. You’re not imagining it—it’s Dr. Dean Olah practicing on his trombone.

“It's just soothing,” Olah shares. “I always like practicing. It's just my time where I can sit and work on something and not worry about anything else.”

In addition to being a Professor of Education, Olah is a professional trombonist who has built an extensive career that seamlessly blends his passions for education and music.

Olah’s foray into music began with an interest to join his school’s band. Growing up in a big family in Toledo, Ohio, he had to ask around the neighborhood to find an instrument he could borrow. He managed to bring home a clarinet and a trombone. The clarinet smelled funny, and its reed was broken, so that left Olah with the trombone.

He started playing in the 5th grade and continued well into high school. Even as he was preparing to attend college, he discovered more opportunities to keep honing his musical skills while also pursuing another lifelong interest.

“I always knew I wanted to be a teacher growing up, but I didn't know what I wanted to teach,” Olah says. “I auditioned at the University of Toledo and got a music scholarship. So I went, ‘okay, I'll teach music.’”

Undergraduate and graduate degrees in music education, along with experience playing other brass instruments like the tuba and the trumpet, allowed Olah to become a band director and teacher at the middle and high school levels, where he could help shape burgeoning young musicians. An additional master's degree in school administration opened the door for him to work as an assistant principal and later a principal. After he earned an EdD in technology education, Olah taught at Campbell University in North Carolina.

Dr. Dean Olah (far left) performs with members of the North Carolina Brass Band during a wedding in 2014. Photo courtesy of Rev. Kayelily Middleton

The classroom was not the only place Olah was able to share his love of music. He played the trombone in several ensembles, including the North Carolina Brass Band, Raleigh Jazz Orchestra, Carolina Philharmonic, and the Moonlighters Big Band.

Olah has also performed with an array of renowned musicians, like Luciano Pavarotti, Dizzy Gillespie, and Barry Manilow, to name a few. “When these famous people go on tour, they come into the cities and put together an orchestra to back them up, and I was one of the ones chosen for that,” he adds.

On top of his group performances, Olah ran a wedding music business with his wife Molly, a violinist whom he met in graduate school. Together, they spent weekends playing at ceremonies and receptions.

“In music, you have to make your own opportunities,” Olah says. “I'm glad we did all that and had all those experiences.”

Dr. Dean Olah and his wife Molly after a performance

Since relocating to Guam in 2015, Olah has continued to stay active in his pedagogical and musical endeavors.

At UOG, Olah is a faculty member with SOE’s Division of Professional Teacher Preparation and is involved in research around educational technology and educational policy. He was part of the team that developed the I Meyeng UOG-Certified Online Teacher Program and has taught summer teacher training classes in Yap and Pohnpei through UOG’s partnership with the College of Micronesia.

Olah also teaches brass music for UOG’s music program, offering trombone and trumpet lessons, and joined Mangilao Hot Jazz, UOG’s official jazz band. Whenever it is a colleague or student’s birthday, he has been known to break out his trumpet to play “Happy Birthday.”

Outside of his university role, Olah is the principal trombonist of the Guam Symphony Orchestra. People still ask him and his wife if they can play at weddings, but lately, they have been more keen on passing the torch along to the next generation of musicians.

“What I like is there are younger people on the island who we can say, ‘You do it, and you make that extra money,’ and it's enjoyable seeing them doing what we used to do,” he says.

Following the Guam Symphony’s 2017 “A Midsummer Night's Dream” concert, Dr. Dean Olah (right) poses with guest conductor Dr. Juyong Kwon and the late Dr. Colleen Jennings.

When asked what the future holds, Olah is playing it by ear, but both teaching and the trombone will remain constants.

“Retirement is my nightmare,” he laughs. “I've got to have something to wake up and look forward to, so yes, I’ll absolutely keep playing, and again, I always wanted to be a teacher, so I'm living the dream.”

Olah’s career, defined by decades of performing on stage and providing guidance for future educators, is a masterclass in following one’s passions fully.

“I don't know how many people get to do that, but I get to wake up every day and do what I enjoy doing,” Olah says.

Dr. Dean Olah (far right) along with other members of GuamBones, the trombone quartet of UOG’s Mangilao Hot Jazz
